# Aim and background

This notebook walks through a basic spatial proteomics analysis in R,
using the example `hyperLOPIT2015` dataset (mouse embryonic stem cells)
from the `pRolocdata` package.

The workflow mirrors the main steps of the *Eimeria tenella* sporozoite
hyperLOPIT study (Attree et al., 2026), so it can be used as training:

1.  Inspect the data and the marker proteins.
2.  Check that marker proteins of the same organelle have similar
    abundance profiles.
3.  Visualise the data with PCA and t-SNE.
4.  Train a **TAGM-MAP** classifier on the markers.
5.  Predict the localisation of the "unknown" proteins.
6.  Keep only confident predictions (localisation probability \>= 0.99).
7.  Compare the result with the results stored in the dataset.

The idea in one paragraph: organelles are separated on a density
gradient, each gradient fraction is measured by TMT mass spectrometry,
so every protein gets an abundance **profile** across fractions.
Proteins in the same organelle have similar profiles. Proteins with
known localisation (**markers**) are used to train a model, which then
predicts the localisation of all other (**unknown**) proteins.

# Installation (run once)

This chunk is **not evaluated** when knitting (`eval = FALSE`). Run it
manually in the R console the first time.

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
# BiocManager is used to install packages from Bioconductor.
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}

# pRoloc:     tools for protein subcellular localisation analysis.
# pRolocdata: example datasets, including hyperLOPIT2015.
# MSnbase:    classes and tools for storing and analysing proteomics data.
# pRolocGUI:  interactive tools for exploring spatial proteomics data.
BiocManager::install(c("pRoloc", "pRolocdata", "MSnbase", "pRolocGUI"))

# Rtsne provides the t-SNE dimensionality reduction method.
install.packages("Rtsne")
```

# Load packages and data

```{r load-packages}
# These packages must be loaded in every new R session.
library(MSnbase)
library(pRoloc)
library(pRolocdata)

# Load the hyperLOPIT2015 dataset (an MSnSet object) from pRolocdata.
data(hyperLOPIT2015)

# Create a shorter name for convenience.
hl <- hyperLOPIT2015

sum(is.na(exprs(hl)))
```

## Overview of the object

An `MSnSet` links three tables:

-   `exprs(hl)`: protein abundance in each sample (the profiles).
-   `fData(hl)`: protein annotations (including the `markers` column).
-   `pData(hl)`: sample annotations (replicate, TMT reagent, gradient
    fraction, density).

```{r overview}
# Summary: number of proteins (features), samples and annotation columns.
hl

# Dimensions of the quantitative data.
# Rows = protein features; columns = samples (replicates x TMT channels).
dims(hl)

# Number of proteins in each marker class.
# "unknown" = proteins without a marker label (these are what we want to predict).
table(fData(hl)$markers)
```

Note the class imbalance: some classes (for example Mitochondrion) have
many markers, while others (for example Endosome) have very few. Small
classes are harder to model well.

The `hyperLOPIT2015` dataset is stored as an `MSnSet` object and
contains quantitative spatial proteomics data. The dataset was
normalized to the sum of intensities.

### Dataset Dimensions

-   **Number of proteins (features):** 5,032
-   **Number of quantitative samples:** 20
-   **Expression data:** `exprs`
-   **Sample metadata:** `phenoData`
-   **Protein metadata:** `featureData`
-   **Publication PMID:** 26754106
-   **MSnbase version recorded in the dataset:** 2.7.5

#### Sample Metadata

The dataset contains 20 quantitative samples across two replicates.
Sample metadata include:

-   `Replicate`
-   `TMT.Reagent`
-   `Acquisition.Method`
-   `Gradient.Fraction`
-   `Iodixonal.Density`

#### Protein Localization Labels

The protein metadata contain localization labels for 5,032 proteins. The
distribution of the labels is summarized below.

| Subcellular compartment               | Number of proteins |
|:--------------------------------------|-------------------:|
| 40S Ribosome                          |                 27 |
| 60S Ribosome                          |                 43 |
| Actin cytoskeleton                    |                 13 |
| Cytosol                               |                 43 |
| Endoplasmic reticulum/Golgi apparatus |                107 |
| Endosome                              |                 13 |
| Extracellular matrix                  |                 13 |
| Lysosome                              |                 33 |
| Mitochondrion                         |                383 |
| Nucleus - Chromatin                   |                 64 |
| Nucleus - Non-chromatin               |                 85 |
| Peroxisome                            |                 17 |
| Plasma membrane                       |                 51 |
| Proteasome                            |                 34 |
| Unknown                               |              4,106 |
| **Total**                             |          **5,032** |

#### Initial Observations

Most proteins (4,106; approximately 81.6%) are labelled `unknown`, while
926 proteins have an assigned subcellular localization label.

**Reference:** Publication associated with the dataset, PMID:
[26754106](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26754106/).

## Sample metadata

```{r pdata}
# Sample metadata: replicate number, TMT reagent, acquisition method,
# gradient fraction and iodixanol density.
# The 20 samples are 2 replicates x 10 fractions. Note that the first sample of
# each replicate is the cytosol (soluble) fraction and one is a chromatin
# fraction, so the x-axis is not a simple continuous density axis.
pData(hl)
```

# Marker classes and their abundance profiles

```{r classes}
# Names of the known localisation classes (the "unknown" label is excluded).
cls <- getMarkerClasses(hl, fcol = "markers")
cls
```

## Mitochondrial markers

```{r profile-mito, fig.height=5}
# Rows of the proteins labelled as Mitochondrion.
i <- which(fData(hl)$markers == "Mitochondrion")

# Make the sample names on the x-axis readable (rotate them, add bottom margin).
# The old graphical settings are saved in `op` and restored afterwards.
op <- par(mar = c(8, 4, 3, 1), las = 2, cex.axis = 0.5)

# Each line is one protein; it shows how its abundance changes across the
# 20 samples. Markers of the same organelle should look alike.
plotDist(hl[i, ], markers = featureNames(hl)[i])

par(op)
```

## Lysosomal markers

```{r profile-lyso, fig.height=5}
# Rows of the proteins labelled as Lysosome.
j <- which(fData(hl)$markers == "Lysosome")

op <- par(mar = c(8, 4, 3, 1), las = 2, cex.axis = 0.5)

# Compare with the mitochondrial plot: the shape is consistent within the
# class but the peak is in a different place. This difference between classes
# is what allows a classifier to tell organelles apart.
plotDist(hl[j, ], markers = featureNames(hl)[j])

par(op)
```

## Mean profile per class

Instead of judging the plots by eye, we can compute the mean profile of
every marker class and find the sample where each class peaks.

```{r mean-profiles}
# Step 1: select the proteins of one marker class.
# Step 2: take their abundance values.
# Step 3: average them for each of the 20 samples.
# Step 4: combine everything into a matrix (rows = classes, columns = samples).
mean.prof <- t(sapply(cls, function(k) {
  colMeans(exprs(hl)[which(fData(hl)$markers == k), ])
}))

# Sample with the highest mean abundance for each class.
colnames(mean.prof)[apply(mean.prof, 1, which.max)]

# The same for two classes we looked at above.
names(which.max(mean.prof["Mitochondrion", ]))
names(which.max(mean.prof["Lysosome", ]))
```

# Dimensionality reduction

## PCA

```{r pca}
# PCA reduces the profiles to a few dimensions that keep as much variation as
# possible. fcol = NULL means we do not colour by marker class yet.
# The percentages on the axes show how much variance each component explains.
plot2D(hl, fcol = NULL, method = "PCA")
```

## t-SNE (no colours)

```{r tsne-plain}
# t-SNE is non-linear and tends to separate clusters more clearly than PCA.
# set.seed() makes the layout reproducible (t-SNE has a random component).
# Important: distances between clusters in t-SNE should not be over-interpreted;
# use it for exploration only.
set.seed(1)
plot2D(hl, fcol = NULL, method = "t-SNE", cex = 0.5)
```

## t-SNE coloured by marker class

```{r tsne-markers}
# Colour proteins by their marker class. Grey points are "unknown" proteins.
# If markers of the same organelle form tight, separate groups, the experiment
# separated the organelles well. This is the equivalent of Fig. 1B in the
# Eimeria paper.
set.seed(1)
plot2D(hl, fcol = "markers", method = "t-SNE", cex = 0.6)

# Legend with the marker-class colours.
addLegend(hl, fcol = "markers", where = "bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.5)
```

```{r tsne-markers-png}
# Save a larger version of the plot as a PNG file (the legend does not overlap
# the data as easily in a bigger figure).
png("tsne_markers.png", width = 1600, height = 1000, res = 150)
set.seed(1)
plot2D(hl, fcol = "markers", method = "t-SNE", cex = 0.6)
addLegend(hl, fcol = "markers", where = "bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.6)
invisible(dev.off())
```

Observations from this plot in our run: mitochondrion, ER/Golgi, the two
nuclear classes, lysosome and the ribosomes form clear groups, whereas
plasma membrane, cytosol, endosome and the very small classes are more
spread out or sparse. A large grey region in the middle contains many
unknown proteins without markers.

# TAGM-MAP classification

TAGM (T-Augmented Gaussian Mixture) is a Bayesian model. It learns the
profile distribution of every marker class and also allows each protein
to be an **outlier** (not belonging to any annotated class). TAGM-MAP is
the fast optimisation version.

## Train the model

```{r tagm-train}
# The values below are the defaults of tagmMapTrain() in our pRoloc version and
# They were not tuned on this dataset.
params <- tagmMapTrain(
  hl,
  fcol    = "markers",  # column with the marker labels
  method  = "MAP",      # maximum a posteriori estimates
  numIter = 100,        # iterations of the EM algorithm
  lambda0 = 0.01,       # prior shrinkage (weak prior)
  u = 2, v = 10,        # Beta prior for the outlier proportion
  seed    = 1           # makes the result reproducible
)
params
```

## Predict localisations

```{r tagm-predict}
# Predict the localisation of all proteins (markers and unknowns).
# probOutlier = TRUE also returns the probability of being an outlier.
res <- tagmMapPredict(hl, params, fcol = "markers", probOutlier = TRUE)

# If tagmMapPredict() is not found in a newer version of pRoloc, use:
# res <- tagmPredict(hl, params, fcol = "markers", probOutlier = TRUE)

# New columns added by the prediction.
fvarLabels(res)

# First proteins: the predicted class, its probability and the outlier probability.
head(fData(res)[, c("markers", "tagm.map.allocation",
                    "tagm.map.probability", "tagm.map.outlier")])
```

How to read these columns:

-   `tagm.map.allocation`: the class the protein is closest to.
-   `tagm.map.probability`: probability of that class.
-   `tagm.map.outlier`: probability that the protein does not belong to
    any class. A protein with an outlier probability near 1 should not
    be trusted, even if an allocation is reported.

```{r prob-outlier-check}
# Sanity check: is probability + outlier close to 1 for all proteins, or only for
# the first few? In our run the median was 1 but the minimum was about 0.50.
fd <- fData(res)
summary(fd$tagm.map.probability + fd$tagm.map.outlier)
```

## Keep only confident predictions

The Eimeria paper combines the two probabilities into one localisation
probability and applies a stringent 0.99 threshold:

localisation probability = allocation probability x (1 - outlier
probability)

```{r threshold}
fd <- fData(res)

# Localisation probability exactly as in the paper (Methods 2.12).
fd$loc.prob <- fd$tagm.map.probability * (1 - fd$tagm.map.outlier)

# Only proteins that were "unknown" are new predictions.
unk <- fd$markers == "unknown"

# Confident new assignments.
keep <- unk & fd$loc.prob >= 0.99

sum(unk)    # unknown proteins we started with (4106 in our run)
sum(keep)   # unknown proteins that passed the 0.99 threshold (1983 in our run)

# Number of new assignments per organelle.
table(fd$tagm.map.allocation[keep])
```

Mitochondrion receives relatively few new assignments because most
mitochondrial proteins are already markers. The very small classes
(extracellular matrix, actin cytoskeleton, peroxisome, proteasome) also
receive few assignments; with only 13 to 34 markers each, the model is
expected to be more conservative for them.

#### Prediction Summary

The TAGM-MAP model was used to predict subcellular localizations for
proteins initially labelled as `unknown`, using a probability threshold
of 0.99.

-   **Initially unknown proteins:** 4,106
-   **Proteins passing the 0.99 threshold:** 1,983
-   **Percentage passing the threshold:** Approximately 48.3%

#### Predicted Subcellular Localization Distribution

The 1,983 proteins that passed the threshold were distributed across the
following subcellular compartments:

| Predicted subcellular compartment     | Number of proteins |
|:--------------------------------------|-------------------:|
| 40S Ribosome                          |                 43 |
| 60S Ribosome                          |                  4 |
| Actin cytoskeleton                    |                  6 |
| Cytosol                               |                332 |
| Endoplasmic reticulum/Golgi apparatus |                250 |
| Endosome                              |                 35 |
| Extracellular matrix                  |                  2 |
| Lysosome                              |                252 |
| Mitochondrion                         |                146 |
| Nucleus - Chromatin                   |                210 |
| Nucleus - Non-chromatin               |                364 |
| Peroxisome                            |                  9 |
| Plasma membrane                       |                321 |
| Proteasome                            |                  9 |

The largest predicted groups were **Nucleus - Non-chromatin (364
proteins)**, **Cytosol (332 proteins)**, and **Plasma membrane (321
proteins)**. These were followed by Lysosome (252 proteins), Endoplasmic
reticulum/Golgi apparatus (250 proteins), and Nucleus - Chromatin (210
proteins).

The remaining 2,123 proteins did not pass the selected threshold. Their
predicted localizations should therefore be treated as lower-confidence
results under this filtering criterion, rather than as confirmed
incorrect predictions.

**Note:** Passing a probability threshold of 0.99 indicates confidence
according to the model's probability measure; it does not independently
confirm the biological localization of a protein.

# Visualise the final assignments

```{r final-labels}
fd <- fData(res)

# Final label for each protein:
#   - a confident prediction (passed the 0.99 threshold), otherwise "unknown";
#   - proteins that were already markers keep their original label.
final <- ifelse(keep, fd$tagm.map.allocation, "unknown")
is.marker <- fd$markers != "unknown"
final[is.marker] <- fd$markers[is.marker]

fData(res)$final <- final
```

```{r tsne-final}
# t-SNE coloured by the final assignment. Compare with the markers-only plot:
# the new assignments fill the regions around the markers, and a grey region of
# unassigned proteins remains in the centre.
set.seed(1)
plot2D(res, fcol = "final", method = "t-SNE", cex = 0.6)
addLegend(res, fcol = "final", where = "bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.5)
```

```{r tsne-final-png}
# Save a larger version as a PNG file.
png("tsne_final.png", width = 1800, height = 1100, res = 150)
set.seed(1)
plot2D(res, fcol = "final", method = "t-SNE", cex = 0.6)
addLegend(res, fcol = "final", where = "bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.6)
invisible(dev.off())
```

The unassigned proteins (those that did not pass 0.99) may have mixed
profiles, may be located in more than one compartment, or may belong to
organelles without markers. The Eimeria paper reports the same kind of
difficult region (HDBSCAN cluster 8, which mixes nucleus, ribosome and
cytosol).

# Validation against the stored results

The dataset contains a table (`TAGM`) with the results from the original
study. We can use it to check that our analysis reproduces them.

```{r stored-table}
# Look at the stored results (MAP and MCMC versions of TAGM).
head(fData(hl)$TAGM)
```

```{r compare}
# Stored results from the original study vs. our results.
old  <- fData(hl)$TAGM
mine <- fData(res)
colnames(old)

# Proteins that were unknown (the real predictions).
unk <- fData(hl)$markers == "unknown"

# 1) Do the allocations agree?
same <- as.character(old[, "tagm.map.allocation"]) ==
        as.character(mine$tagm.map.allocation)
mean(same)        # fraction of all proteins that agree (0.994 in our run)
mean(same[unk])   # fraction of unknown proteins that agree (0.993 in our run)

# 2) How similar are the probabilities?
old.p <- as.numeric(old[, "tagm.map.probability"])
cor(old.p, mine$tagm.map.probability, use = "complete.obs")   # 0.998 in our run
plot(old.p, mine$tagm.map.probability,
     xlab = "Stored MAP probability", ylab = "My MAP probability")
```

The comparison between the stored MAP results and the newly generated
predictions produced the following results:

| Evaluation metric                                                         | Result |
|:-----------------------------------|-----------------------------------:|
| Agreement in localization assignments across all proteins                 | 99.44% |
| Agreement in assignments among initially unknown proteins                 | 99.32% |
| Pearson correlation between stored and newly calculated MAP probabilities | 0.9982 |
| Number of proteins with different localization assignments                |     28 |

#### Interpretation

The newly generated TAGM-MAP predictions showed high agreement with the
stored results. Approximately 99.44% of all proteins received the same
localization assignment, while agreement among proteins initially
labelled as `unknown` was approximately 99.32%.

The Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9982 indicates a very strong
positive linear relationship between the stored and newly calculated MAP
probabilities.

Although the localization assignments differed for 28 proteins, all 28
were initially labelled as `unknown`. These differences may reflect
variations in model fitting or parameter estimation and do not, by
themselves, indicate which localization is biologically correct.

```{r disagreements}
# 3) Proteins where the two analyses disagree (28 in our run).
d <- which(!same)
length(d)

data.frame(
  stored   = old[d, "tagm.map.allocation"],
  mine     = mine$tagm.map.allocation[d],
  stored.p = old.p[d],
  my.p     = mine$tagm.map.probability[d]
)
```

In most of the disagreeing proteins both probabilities are extremely
small, so the reported allocation is just the "least unlikely" class and
a tiny numerical difference can change it. Always look at the
probability, not only at the allocation.

```{r disagreements-threshold}
# Do any of the disagreeing proteins pass the 0.99 threshold in our results?
# If not (expected: 0), the final confident list is not affected by them.
loc.prob <- mine$tagm.map.probability * (1 - mine$tagm.map.outlier)
sum(loc.prob[d] >= 0.99)
max(loc.prob[d])   # highest localisation probability among the disagreeing proteins
```
